speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: asked	the Minister for Social and Family Development (a) what is the number of people who have committed suicide or attempted suicide each year in the past five years; (b) how many were aged 60 and above; (c) how many of these seniors were living by themselves and how many were living with their families; and (d) what resources and programmes are currently in place to help to address the likely causes of such suicides and to prevent the suicide rates from increasing.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: As the causes of suicides are complex and multi-faceted, we do need to take a holistic perspective when we examine and try to review each individual suicide and to see how we should approach it.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Why it seems a lot more visible today, I guess a lot of it has got to do with media, especially social media.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: When news breaks, stories sometimes are shared in various forums.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: It is circulated and a lot more awareness is there.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: But when we look at the numbers themselves, the trends are not picking up in a big way.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: It does not mean that it is not important because every life lost via suicide is one death too many and we should endeavour to try to prevent it.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Essentially, there are four ways in which we want to approach this.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Under the Seniors Health Curriculum, which is rolled out by the Health Promotion Board (HPB), this is part of our National Seniors' Health Programme where seniors are taught socioemotional and self-care skills and how to seek help if necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: HPB also conducts workshops in workplaces to educate Singaporeans, in particular mature workers, on mental resilience and well-being.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: The Agency for Integrated Care (AIC) also works with community-based organisations, including the SACs, to support seniors who may be at risk of depression and dementia via the Community Resource, Engagement and Support Teams (CREST) programme.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: It is part of the Community Befriending Programme that volunteer befrienders visit seniors regularly to prevent social isolation and support their needs.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: This is something that all of us as individuals can do.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We really should think about mobilising our residents and volunteers to play a part in this effort because it is really about picking up information, picking tell-tale signs and providing social support where we can.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Of course, Family Service Centres (FSCs) support families and individuals, including seniors, through casework and counselling to resolve their relationship, financial, emotional difficulties and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Those in distress or who are facing crises do call the Samaritans of Singapore, which operates a 24-hour hotline.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: The Institute of Mental Health also operates a 24-hour Mental Health Helpline manned by counsellors who can assess and after that triage cases, and activate home visit teams if necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Lastly, while all these initiatives are important, the most critical role really is played by the individuals themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Families, let us not forget the role that families play; and, of course, the community, the people who live around us.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: At the individual level, individuals should take personal responsibility.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: They need to raise self-awareness, be self-aware and recognise tell-tale signs so that they can seek help early when feeling overwhelmed and emotionally distressed.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Family members must help to pick up signs of distress and render emotional support, or help the troubled family member to seek professional assistance early.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Co-workers, colleagues at work, friends and neighbours can also play a very important role in offering assistance and support to those facing life's challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Without these steps, even the best support programmes that we put in place will be rendered ineffective.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: So, we must all step forward and play an active part in looking out for our fellow Singaporeans, our loved ones and together with the rest of the other programmes we have put in place, I think we will have a good shot at reaching out to those who need help.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the issue of social isolation, I understand from press reports that there has been a huge number of increase, over the last, say, 15 years, in the number of elderly people living alone compared to 15 years ago.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am particularly addressing people who live alone and whose spouses have passed on.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand from my grassroots activities that some of these elderly do not want to be involved in some of these current activities at the SACs and other activity centres.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am just wondering whether the Ministry will consider taking a new approach to some form of befriender programme or something to interact with these elderly whose partners have passed on and to provide social company and to try to reintegrate them into society.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I think it is a very real concern for a number of reasons.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The other factor that we are all familiar with is  that family structures are also changing.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: So, sometimes, you may have children but they may be working abroad or, sometimes, in some cases, you do have strained relationships.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: So, you will gradually begin to see, of course, one, more elderly and, of course, there are the elderly who are living alone for a range of reasons and you will also correspondingly see some of these numbers increase.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But certainly, isolation, I do not think it is necessarily a good thing either because people do need to be socially engaged.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: They may be living alone but it does not mean that they are necessarily socially engaged.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: They may be in contact with their family, their regular social activities.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But they can become a concern at some point where they become less mobile, when they become less able to meet up with other people.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Which is why it is very important for us to realise that the grassroots activities are very important.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Ultimately, at some stage, your neighbours and the community in which you live in become very critical.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Family members are there, and that is always the first line.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: That is critical and we hope that families continue to visit.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Which is why we also want to redefine the sort of family structure and look beyond just the nuclear family; the extended family becomes important − cousins, nephews, uncles, aunts.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We need to nurture that extended family relationship as well.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Relationships within a family do not just automatically happen.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We also need to put in the effort to make sure that at least that part in terms of providing emotional support to their elderly and to family members remains.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: As Members know, some of the activities that we have, we have the same old people taking part in the activities.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We want new old people to take part.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: And the Member is right that some do not participate, for a range of reasons.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Sometimes, they may have just moved in, there is no social connection with the local community as yet.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: That is a very important part of our programme in terms of outreach; slowly getting to know who are those people who are isolated, and then how do we begin to get to know them and slowly begin to connect them with the community at large and begin to get them out of their homes and to participate in activities.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Once that ice is broken, we can begin to see some of them beginning to play an active role.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: There are some who do not want to come out, again, for a range of reasons.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: That is something I am exploring as well, because companies are looking at corporate social responsibility efforts.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Sometimes, we may be looking for some big-bang activities.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Indeed, the partnership between MSF and MOH is critical.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It is very hard to just draw a line that this is a social issue, this is a health issue.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I would say the third factor is a community issue.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: So, the grassroots organisations and structure are a very valuable set-up.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The PG office is particularly important because they are actively visiting the PG.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We are also picking up information from them because they sometimes notice that elderly folks are just so happy to have someone to talk to.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: These are not the elderly folks living on their own.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This suggests to us that, sometimes, they may be living with their older parents but they are not being engaged or are being disregarded in some ways.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: That is something we are focusing on to see how to operationalise this.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Some of us are doing this on the ground as Members of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I have spoken to a number of you on some of the possible outreach efforts that can be done and I do sincerely believe that this is possible.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It is really a question of us organising ourselves at the ground level to do this.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: No shortage of outreach efforts, but I think we need to work together to collaborate.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In my experience working with the elderly, I realise that language plays a very important part in communication.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I wonder if all of MSF's outreach programmes would also include other languages.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Besides English, which most of the organisations are comfortable with, we are really looking at Mandarin, Malay, Tamil or even various dialects.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And how do we make sure that these are going out to the elderly?

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We work closely with the getai community to get some of the messages out.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Dialects become important, as well as Malay, Tamil and so on.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We are looking out for volunteers from different backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I would urge the different communities to step forward to play a part because we do need to leverage on your language skills.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We do have people who want to reach out.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But sometimes there is an impediment because of language.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It definitely helps once again to call out for those who are from different backgrounds to play a part, because that is important.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I am sure you have seen a lot of the Hokkien and various advertisements which have gone down very well with the elderly.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I know some people are a bit ‒ for want of a better word ‒ kind of scornful about "Why do you have this kind of videos?

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But it is different strokes for different folks.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We may not always relate to some of these types of programmes and collaterals, but it reaches out to different segments of our society.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The key thing, as far as we are concerned, is that it does not matter what the platform is.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Get the message out and then enable individuals to then look after themselves as well, and also to encourage those around them to do that.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Language plays a very important role, particularly presently when a lot of the elderly, perhaps because of their education level where their language competencies are not quite the same.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: As we go forward in the next 10, 15 years, this issue should be less acute.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: A lot more people should be able to speak the main languages.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But it is something that we still need to look out for.
